description: Red Team Village at DEF CON 27 covers offensive security techniques, red team tactics, and adversarial operations. The talks explore implant automation, red team frameworks, detection evasion, data center attacks, and adversarial DevOps practices.

talks.title: SiestaTime Automation fr Long term implants
talks.teaser: SiestaTime Automation fr Long term implants
talks.summary:
In this technical session at the DEF CON 27 Red Team Village, Alvaro Folgado introduces "SiestaTime," an automated framework designed to manage and orchestrate long-term persistent implants during extended adversary emulation engagements. He begins at 05:00 by demonstrating how SiestaTime automates the provisioning of disposable cloud infrastructure across AWS and DigitalOcean, dynamically generating redirectors, domains, and virtual private servers on demand.

Alvaro dives into covert communication channels at 10:00, explaining how SiestaTime maintains stealthy access while bypassing corporate firewalls and intrusion detection systems. At 15:00, he presents out-of-band staging mechanisms and dead-drop resolvers, showcasing an evasion technique at 20:00 that utilizes web-based services like Gmail drafts as an asynchronous command-and-control channel where messages are read without ever transmitting an outbound SMTP email.

Turning to defensive evasion at 25:00, Alvaro discusses how randomized beacon jitter and extended hibernation cycles prevent network security monitoring tools from establishing behavioral baselines. He concludes at 30:00 by releasing the tool to the security community, offering guidance on safely automating implant staging while avoiding common network hygiene mistakes during prolonged enterprise red team operations. talks.title: Red Team Framework RTF
talks.summary:
Adrian Sanabria introduces the Red Team Framework (RTF), an open methodology developed to bring structure, consistency, and objective-based measurement to adversary emulation engagements and collaborative offensive security operations.

[03:00] Sanabria begins by clarifying foundational industry definitions, distinguishing between vulnerability scanning, compliance penetration testing, red teaming, and purple teaming. He critiques the conventional compliance-focused checklist model, pointing out that automated Nessus scans provide little insight into whether an enterprise can withstand targeted attacks. He argues that red team operations must be driven by business-aligned objectives [17:03], such as evaluating lateral movement restrictions, measuring the time required to pivot from web systems into financial records, or assessing domain controller defensibility.

[31:06] The presentation outlines the core stages of the RTF, from pre-engagement planning and threat modeling to execution and collaborative debriefing. Sanabria stresses the importance of eliminating the adversarial "gotcha" mentality, advocating that red teams actively partner with blue teams to develop defensive roadmaps and improve detection visibility. He explores key operational metrics [51:28]—including time-to-detection, time-to-containment, and lateral movement friction—and highlights how automated breach-impact assessments [01:03:42] allow organizations to continuously evaluate security postures against evolving adversary tradecraft.

talks.title: Casting with the Pros Tips and Tricks
talks.teaser: Casting with the Pros Tips and Tricks
talks.summary:
In this presentation at the DEF CON 27 Red Team Village, Nathan Sweaney shares advanced social engineering methodologies and tradecraft for professional red team operations. He begins at 06:00 by emphasizing the importance of high-fidelity threat emulation, explaining that realistic assessments must mirror sophisticated adversary playbooks to properly evaluate an organization's defense-in-depth posture from external perimeter to internal domain controller.

Nathan discusses analyzing workflow bottlenecks and policy gaps at 12:00, showing how defenders often rely on technical controls that degrade under operational pressure. At 18:00, he demonstrates chaining web application vulnerabilities with targeted phishing campaigns, using Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) on trusted partner portals to execute authenticated actions. At 24:00, he illustrates weaponizing Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) via phishing links, executing an administrative API call that silently adds a red team account into the Domain Admins active directory group.

Addressing corporate context at 30:00, Nathan recounts working with executives following high-profile incidents like the OPM breach, explaining how to communicate systemic risk without inducing organizational paralysis. He finishes at 36:00 by demonstrating how to craft email templates that evade advanced threat protection filters and spam gateways, emphasizing that testing must validate human reporting mechanisms alongside technical perimeter controls. talks.title: BadSalt Adversarial DevOps
talks.summary:
Casey Erdmann explores the offensive capabilities of enterprise configuration management tools, presenting "BadSalt"—a research project and toolset demonstrating how SaltStack infrastructure can be leveraged by red teams and adversaries for stealthy command-and-control (C2) and automated post-exploitation.

[05:25] Erdmann explains the underlying architecture of SaltStack, detailing how the Salt Master communicates with distributed Minion agents across ZeroMQ publish and request ports (4505 and 4506). He examines the cryptographic authentication model, highlighting security risks during minion bootstrapping where missing or unverified master key fingerprints enable man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks [15:20] that allow an attacker to hijack agent connections.

[22:01] The presentation highlights the evasion benefits of living off the land with legitimate, enterprise-signed Salt minion software. Because Salt agents are trusted administrative tools, they routinely bypass endpoint detection and response (EDR) and antivirus software. Erdmann demonstrates using declarative Salt state files (.sls) [26:03] to automate complex post-exploitation tasks across thousands of systems simultaneously, such as adding persistent administrative backdoor accounts, reconfiguring local firewalls, and establishing secondary access. He concludes by analyzing SaltStack network traffic patterns [32:55] and logging artifacts, providing blue teams with actionable detection strategies to identify rogue configuration activity.
